testCases.name: test_case_0
testCases.input: why can't we test an LLM app the same way we test normal software?
testCases.actualOutput:
Because the very nature of an LLM‑based application is different from that of a conventional piece of software. Traditional software is deterministic: if you give it the same input, it will always produce the same output. That means you can write a handful of test cases, run them, and immediately see whether the program behaves as expected. If a test fails, you know exactly what went wrong and you can fix it.

An LLM, on the other hand, is probabilistic. Even when you feed it the exact same prompt, the model can generate different responses each time. That variability means that a single test case can’t simply “pass” or “fail” in the same binary way. Instead, you have to consider a range of possible outputs and evaluate them against a set of criteria—accuracy, relevance, safety, alignment with source material, and so on. You also need to run the same test set on multiple versions of the model to see whether performance is improving, which requires repeatability and a carefully constructed dataset.

Because of this inherent randomness and the need for nuanced, multi‑dimensional criteria, you can’t rely on the straightforward, deterministic test‑case approach that works for ordinary software. Evaluating an LLM app demands a more elaborate, repeatable, and criteria‑driven methodology.
testCases.expectedOutput: Normal software is deterministic and rule-based, so the same input always gives the same output and you can assert one exact expected value. LLM applications are probabilistic, so the same input can produce different wordings, and most tasks have many acceptable answers instead of one exact string. That breaks exact-match testing, so LLM evaluation instead judges qualities of the output, usually against a golden dataset and often with an LLM as a judge.

testCases.name: test_case_1
testCases.input: what's the difference between model evals and application evals?
testCases.actualOutput:
Model evals and application evals are two ways of testing an LLM, but they look at different things.  
Model evals are all about the model itself. They run the LLM on a set of standardized benchmarks—things that measure knowledge, reasoning, math, and other core capabilities. When a new LLM comes out, people run these benchmarks to see how it stacks up against others and to publish a score or leaderboard position. If you need to pick a model for a particular job, you can also run custom model evals: you create your own dataset that reflects the tasks you care about and see which model performs best. In short, model evals answer the question, “How good is this LLM at the kinds of tasks it was trained for?”

Application evals, on the other hand, evaluate the whole system that uses the LLM. They test an LLM‑powered application—say a chatbot, a recommendation engine, or a chart‑building tool—to see how well it works in practice. The goal is to judge the application’s performance, not just the raw model. Application evals can also use custom tests, deep eval, or the LMEvaluation harness to run the application against a benchmark that reflects real‑world usage. So while model evals focus on the LLM’s intrinsic abilities, application evals focus on how those abilities translate into a finished product.
testCases.expectedOutput: Model evals test the capabilities of the raw LLM itself, independent of any product, and include benchmarks as well as custom model evals used to pick a model. Application evals test a system built around one or more LLMs, such as a RAG chatbot or an agent, evaluated end-to-end. In short, model evals judge the model, application evals judge the system you built.

testCases.name: test_case_2
testCases.input: what are the different methods to actually perform an eval?
testCases.actualOutput: The course has outlined three distinct ways to carry out an evaluation. First, you can use **programmatic methods**—writing code that automatically computes metrics such as accuracy or other quantitative scores. Second, you can employ an **LLM‑based judge** through tools like the LLMEval harness, where the language model itself acts as the evaluator. Third, you can conduct **human evaluation**, having people read the model’s outputs and judge them directly. These three approaches—programmatic, LLM‑judge, and human—cover the full range of evaluation methods discussed in the material.
testCases.expectedOutput: There are three broad methods. Programmatic (deterministic) evaluation uses code and fixed rules to check the output, which is cheap and reliable but only works when correctness can be expressed in code. LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable LLM to score outputs, which handles subjective or semantic judgments at scale. Human evaluation uses people to judge outputs, which is the most reliable for nuanced quality but the slowest and most expensive.
